questions.explanation: Dividing two ints truncates to an int, so a / b is 3, and a % b is the remainder, 1. The cast applies to a before the division, so (double) a / b is 3.5; (double) (a / b) would be 3.0.

questions.code:
int max = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
System.out.println(max + 1 == Integer.MIN_VALUE);
questions.explanation: int arithmetic wraps around silently when it overflows, so MAX_VALUE + 1 is MIN_VALUE. Math.addExact throws an ArithmeticException instead, or use a long.

questions.code: System.out.println(1 + 2 + "3" + 4 + 5);
questions.explanation: + is evaluated left to right. 1 + 2 is the int 3; adding "3" makes a String, and from then on every + is concatenation: "33", "334", "3345".

questions.prompt: What does this print, line by line?
questions.explanation: A compound assignment casts its result back to the variable's type, so c += 1 compiles and makes c 'b' (c = c + 1 would not compile). In 'a' + 1 the char is promoted to int, so println gets the int 98.
x++ gives 5 and then makes x 6; ++x makes x 7 and gives 7. So y is 5 + 7 = 12, and x ends at 7.

questions.prompt: What does this print, line by line?
questions.explanation: 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary form, so the double sum is 0.30000000000000004 and is not == 0.3. BigDecimal built from strings does exact decimal arithmetic, so 0.1 + 0.2 equals 0.3; use it for money.

String literals are interned, so a and b are the same object. new String always makes a separate object, so == (same object?) is false while equals (same characters?) is true. Compare strings with equals.

questions.prompt: What does this print, with default JVM settings?
questions.explanation: Autoboxing calls Integer.valueOf, which caches -128 to 127, so a and b are the same object. Each 128 is a new object, and == compares references. Compare boxed numbers with equals, or unbox them.

Strings are immutable: replace returns a new string, which is thrown away here, and s still refers to "java". Write s = s.replace("a", "o"); to keep the result, which is jovo, since replace changes every match.

questions.prompt: Which is the efficient way to build a long string inside a loop?
options: A StringBuilder, calling append() in the loop
questions.answer: A StringBuilder, calling append() in the loop
questions.explanation: Each += or concat makes a new String and copies everything built so far, which is quadratic over the loop. A StringBuilder appends into one growing buffer. The compiler optimises a single + expression, but not across loop iterations.

questions.code:
String csv = "a,b,,c,,";
System.out.println(csv.split(",").length);
questions.explanation: split keeps the empty strings between delimiters but drops the trailing ones, leaving a, b, the empty string and c. Pass a negative limit, split(",", -1), to keep them all (6 here).

Line 2 checks for null before calling length(), and on line 3 equals is called on the literal, which simply returns false for null. Line 4 calls a method on null and throws NullPointerException; write "root".equals(name) or Objects.equals(name, "root").
Instance methods are dispatched on the object's runtime class, not the variable's declared type, so Cat's override runs.

Overloads are chosen at compile time from the declared types of the arguments. value is declared Object, so print(Object) is picked even though it holds a String. Overriding is what is decided at run time.

questions.prompt: Which statement about this code is true?
options: It compiles, and new Square().name() returns shape
Square must override name() to compile
Shape can be created with new Shape()
A class cannot both extend a class and implement an interface
questions.answer: It compiles, and new Square().name() returns shape
questions.explanation: A default method gives implementing classes a working method they may override but need not. An abstract class cannot be instantiated, and a class can extend one class while implementing any number of interfaces.
A static field belongs to the class, so all three constructors increment the same count. Each account stores the value it saw, and the third account's id is 3.

questions.prompt: You override equals() in a class used as a HashMap key. What else must you override?
questions.explanation: HashMap finds the bucket by hashCode before it calls equals. Equal objects must have equal hash codes, or looking up with an equal key can miss the entry.

A record generates equals, hashCode and toString from its components, so two records with the same values are equal, and toString looks like Point[x=1, y=2]. == still compares references, and these are two objects.
Removing from a list while a for-each loop iterates over it makes the loop's iterator fail fast on its next step. Use nums.removeIf(n -> n % 2 == 0), or an explicit Iterator and its remove().

questions.prompt: What is the average time complexity of HashMap.get, and of ArrayList.contains, with n elements?
questions.explanation: HashMap hashes the key straight to a bucket, constant time on average. ArrayList.contains walks the list calling equals on each element until it finds a match.

questions.code:
List<String> names = List.of("ann", "bob");
names.add("cy");
questions.explanation: List.of returns an unmodifiable list: add, remove and set all throw UnsupportedOperationException. Copy it into a new ArrayList<>(...) when you need to change it.
merge stores 1 for a new key and otherwise combines the old and new values with Integer::sum, so a reaches 2. getOrDefault returns the default for a missing key instead of null.

questions.prompt: Which map keeps its keys sorted, with O(log n) get and put?
questions.explanation: TreeMap is a red-black tree ordered by the keys' natural order or a Comparator, so get and put are O(log n). HashMap has no order, LinkedHashMap keeps insertion order, and Hashtable is the legacy synchronised HashMap.
remove(int) removes by index, so remove(1) takes out 20. remove(Object) removes by value, so remove(Integer.valueOf(10)) then takes out 10.
A return in finally replaces the try block's return value, and would swallow an exception too. That is why returning from finally is a well-known mistake (javac warns about it).

questions.prompt: Which of these is a checked exception, one a method must catch or declare?
questions.explanation: Checked exceptions extend Exception but not RuntimeException, and the compiler makes you catch or declare them. The other three extend RuntimeException, so they are unchecked.

questions.prompt: Which is the idiomatic way to make sure a reader is closed, even if reading throws?
options: Call reader.close() at the end of the try block
Close it in a catch (Exception e) block
Leave it to the garbage collector
questions.explanation: try-with-resources closes everything it declares when the block exits, normally or by an exception, and keeps any exception from close() as suppressed. A close() at the end of the try is skipped when something throws, and a catch block only runs on failure.

questions.prompt: What does this print, line by line?
options: class cast, then runtime, then finally
questions.explanation: Casting a String to Integer throws ClassCastException. Only the first matching catch runs, even though RuntimeException would also match, and finally runs afterwards either way.

questions.prompt: riskyCall() is declared to throw IOException. Does this compile?
options: No: the IOException catch can never be reached
Yes, and an IOException goes to the second catch
Yes, and both catches run for an IOException
questions.answer: No: the IOException catch can never be reached
questions.explanation: Catch blocks are tried in order, and catch (Exception e) already catches every IOException, so the compiler rejects the later, narrower catch: exception IOException has already been caught. Put the more specific catch first.

Both calls run, each printing "done " from its finally, before println receives their sum. parse("x") catches the NumberFormatException and returns -1, so the sum is 42 + -1 = 41: two ints, not strings.
filter keeps the odd numbers 1, 3 and 5, and map squares them. toList() (Java 16+) collects the result into an unmodifiable list.

options: It prints ab, then throws an IllegalStateException
questions.answer: It prints ab, then throws an IllegalStateException
questions.explanation: A stream can be consumed only once. The second terminal operation throws IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed. Stream again from the source collection, or from a Supplier<Stream<String>>.
Intermediate operations are lazy: they run only when a terminal operation, such as toList() or forEach, pulls elements through. This pipeline has none, so peek never runs.
groupingBy puts each word in the list for its length, in encounter order, so length 2 holds hi and yo. No word has 4 letters, so get returns null rather than an empty list.

questions.prompt: findUser(id) returns Optional<User>. Which is the idiomatic way to get the user's email, or "none"?
questions.explanation: map transforms the value when there is one and orElse supplies the fallback, with no null checks. get() throws NoSuchElementException on an empty Optional, an Optional itself is never meant to be null, and Optional has no email() method.
rangeClosed includes its end, so it sums 1 to 4, which is 10. range excludes its end, so it yields 1, 2 and 3: a count of 3.
